add_to_this_grid: A new cube on the same grid as the form being edited, set down beside what is there. Forms on one grid are kept clear of each other and turn together. Choose another kind from Form, or drag the cube's dots to make it a floor or a wall.
arch_askew: This arch runs at an angle to the brick grid: its feet differ along both X and Y. No flat outline can be fitted to it, so it is fitted cell by cell and comes out stepped.
arch_hedge: The arch is grown as the Plant form's hedge: tufts of leaves over every face of its band, filled inside, light on top and dark underneath, on stems at its two feet. A hedge cannot be thinner than 6 microbricks, so an arch thinner or less deep than that is built 6 thick and 6 deep. The opening keeps the plain arch's shape, and the leaves stand into it by one microbrick at the most. Filled has no effect on an arch of hedge.
arch_kind: The shape of the arch between its two feet.
bezier_pull: How strongly this point draws the curve towards itself. 1 is neutral.
blend: How far the join between this form and the forms it stands in is rounded, in microbricks along each of them. At 0 the two meet in a sharp crease. The bricks are fitted afresh where the forms meet and are each form's own everywhere else. A form is joined by moving it into another with Ctrl held, and then moves a whole microbrick at a time, so that its bricks line up with those of the form it joins.
bloom_fallen: A few loose petals lying on the floor beside the bloom, on the side it faces when it is tipped over.
bloom_flower: Which flower the bloom is. A rose is a high-centred double rose, its heart furled and its outer petals cupped with rolled lips. A water lily is a star of pointed petals round yellow stamens. A gerbera is two rows of rays round a disc. Choosing one changes the colours to those it starts in, if the colours were still the last flower's own.
bloom_stem: A short length of stem behind the bloom, for a cut flower laid down. The bloom rests on it where it is lowest.
bloom_tilt: How far the bloom is tipped over from facing straight up, in degrees. At 0 it faces the sky and at 90 it lies on its side. It is grown along the slant, so its bricks stay on the grid, and it is set down on whatever part of it is then lowest, which may be its petals, its sepals or its stem.
bloom_turn: Which way round the bloom is tipped, in degrees: 0 is towards +X and 90 towards +Y. With no tilt it turns the bloom about its own middle.
brick_budget: The smallest brick size that keeps the build within this many bricks is used. A form laid as a pattern of tiles is not held to it, and nor is a plant: both are built at single microbricks unless you set a Brick size.
brick_size: Fits the form with bricks a multiple of this size. Automatic picks the finest size that keeps the build within the brick budget.
carve: Takes this form away from the forms it is joined to and builds none of its own bricks: a window through a wall, a hole through a sphere. The form is drawn as red glass so that it can still be seen and moved. Blend then rounds the rim of the hole. Untick it and the form is added to the others again.
cherry_petals: Ticked, fallen petals lie scattered on the ground under the cherry's crown, thickest under its middle.
claude_command: Run this once in a terminal to tell Claude Code where the editor is. After that, start Claude Code, tick the box above, and ask it to build something.
claude_on: Lets Claude add, change, colour, turn and remove forms in this workspace while you watch, through the Model Context Protocol. Off until you tick it, and off again each time the program starts. While it is on, the editor listens on this computer only; every change Claude makes is named at the top of the view and can be taken back with Ctrl+Z.
clear_reports: Deletes every saved report file. Nothing else is touched.
closed_loop: Joins the last point back to the first.
colour_mode: How the form is coloured: one colour, a blend from one colour to another, stripes, or as its pattern has it. Each brick is one colour.
colour_runs_along: The direction a blend or stripes run in across the form.
colours: The colours used. Click one to change it. A blend or stripes take up to four and a pattern or a form with parts of its own up to 32, added with + and taken away with -. Right-click a colour to copy it, and right-click another to paste it there.
copy_to_clipboard: Writes the form being edited, and any others marked +, to brickloft-build.brz, a Brickadia prefab file, and puts that file on the clipboard. Ctrl+C does the same, and Ctrl+V adds the forms of a copied file back to the workspace.
cube_size: How long the cube is along this axis, in whole microbricks. Its middle stays where it is. To move one side alone, drag the dot on it. A pattern is laid through the shortest of the three lengths, so it shows on the largest face.
depth: How deep a flat band is, measured across the plane its curve lies in.
discrepancy: The volume where the bricks and the true form disagree: missing material plus extra material.
dots_move: Which way a dragged dot moves: in the plane facing the camera, or with one of its coordinates kept as it is.
duplicate_form: A copy of the form being edited on the same grid, coloured the same, set down beside it. Ctrl+D does the same.
facing: The axis the circle faces along. Z lays it flat.
fill_curve: Fills everything the curve encloses: a ring becomes a disc, an arch a filled arch.
flip: Mirror the finished form along an axis, about the middle of its points.
floor_below_form: Lowers the floor in the view so you can look at a form from underneath. The floor is also see-through from below. It changes nothing that is built.
form: The kind of form to build. Choosing one starts it at its usual size.
furniture_back: A thin panel closing the back, in the second of the two wood colours. Unticked, the bookcase is open behind and can be seen through.
furniture_bay: The widest an opening may be, in microbricks. A bookcase wider than this inside is divided by uprights into the fewest equal bays that are no wider.
furniture_board: How thick the sides, top, shelves and uprights are, in microbricks. Boards are made thinner where the bookcase is too small for them.
furniture_books: How full the shelves are, from bare to packed. Books stand in runs against the sides of each bay, with the room left over beside them; here and there one leans, a few lie in a pile, or an ornament stands in the gap. Each book is one brick in one of six colours.
furniture_choice:
dining, coffee, side: What the table stands on. Square legs; legs that taper to the floor on their two inner faces; turned legs with a ball and a neck; a trestle at each end with a rail between; or one pedestal under the middle. A leg too thin for its kind is square.
desk: What the end without drawers stands on: square, tapered or turned legs.
chair, bench: What fills the back between its two posts. Slats stand upright between two rails; a ladder back is rails across; a panel is solid; spindles run from the seat to a deep top rail.
stool: Whether the seat is square or round. A round seat has its corners cut at 45 degrees.
armchair, sofa: Square arms, or rolled ones whose tops slope away outwards.
cupboard, drawers, sideboard, kitchen: Knobs, bars, or no handles at all. Handles are metal in the game.
tablelamp, floorlamp, pendant, sconce: The shape of the shade. A drum is a straight-sided ring round the light, a cone slopes in towards its top, and a globe is light all through.
bed: The headboard. A solid panel, upright slats between two rails, or rails across.
potted: The pot. A terracotta pot with a rim and a saucer, a straight glazed pot with a band, a square planter on feet, or a tall planter that leans out to its top.
trellis: The lattice. Square: uprights with rails across in front of them. Diamond: laths at 45 degrees each way inside a frame, made of sloped bricks. Arched: a square lattice whose top is a stepped arch.
painting: What the painting is of. A sunset over water, with the sun on the horizon and its reflection under it; a landscape of hills one behind another, with firs, and on some seeds mountains or a lake; or an abstract of rectangles, bands or arcs. Each subject has its own sets of colours.
portrait: What the sitter wears: nothing, glasses, a hat or a beard. The seed picks the sitter: the shape of the head, the skin, the hair and its colour, the clothes and the smile.
furniture_colours: A set of colours for the piece. A bookcase has its own: the wood, a second tone for the back panel, and six that the books share. Every other kind takes its style's sets, which are for what things are made of: the wood, a second wood or the paint of doors, metal, upholstery, a second cloth, the light of a lamp, pale linen, and a top of another stuff. A plant in a pot has the pot, its rim (on a trellis the lattice), the soil, stems, two greens and two colours of flower. A picture has its frame, a liner and a mount, and then the colours of its subject: a sunset's sky from its top down, a sitter's skin, hair and clothes. Change any colour below to make a set of your own.
furniture_divided: Ticked, a bookcase wider than Widest bay is divided by uprights. Unticked, its shelves run the whole width in one span.
furniture_kind: Which piece of furniture, in groups: storage, tables, seating, lights, beds, plants in pots, and pictures. Choosing one starts it at its usual size, and keeps the style and seed, so a chair made from a table of a set is a chair of that set.
furniture_moulding: A cornice under an overhanging top and a skirting round the foot, on the front and both sides, each a plain chamfer made of sloped bricks. The carcass is set in by their depth, so the size stays the size of the whole. With Use ramps and corner pieces unticked they are square bands.
furniture_plinth: How far the bottom shelf is lifted off the floor, in microbricks, on a recessed kick board. At 0 the bottom board stands on the floor.
furniture_count:
desk: How many drawers each pedestal has, one above another. By its size is one for every six microbricks of height.
sofa: How many seat cushions, each with a back cushion. By its size is one for each stretch as wide as the seat is deep.
cupboard: How many doors stand side by side. By its size is one for every fourteen microbricks of width.
drawers: How many drawers, one above another, the deepest at the bottom. By its size is one for every six microbricks of height.
sideboard: How many doors and stacks of drawers stand side by side. By its size is one for every thirteen microbricks of width.
kitchen: How many units stand side by side under the one worktop. By its size is one for every ten microbricks of width.
potted, windowbox: How much of the whole height the pot takes, in tenths. By its size is three tenths, and nearly half for a tall planter.
trellis: How many microbricks are left between one slat and the next. By its size is about a seventh of its width.
furniture_extra:
dining: Rails low down between the legs: one from front to back at each end, and one along the middle joining them. Some styles have them whether this is ticked or not.
coffee: A shelf between the legs, a quarter of the way up.
side: A drawer under the top, with a knob.
desk: A pedestal of drawers at both ends, where the desk is wide enough to leave room for knees between them. Unticked, one end has drawers and the other two legs.
chair: Arms: the front legs carried up, and a rail from each to the back.
bench: A back, as a chair has. The height is then the height of the back, and the seat is a little under half way up.
cupboard: A row of drawers along the foot, one under each pair of doors.
drawers: The top drawer as two small ones side by side.
sideboard: Drawers in the middle and doors at each end, where it has three parts or more.
kitchen: A drawer over the door of every unit.
bed: A footboard, a little higher than the mattress.
potted, basket, windowbox, trellis: Ticked, the plant's leaves and flowers are written to the game with their collision off, so a player walks through them; the pot, the soil, the stems and the trellis stay solid.
painting, portrait: A mount between the frame and the picture, in a colour of its own. The picture is smaller by it.
furniture_match: Gives every other piece of furniture in the workspace this one's style, seed and colours. Pieces of one style and seed share their legs, their weight and their woods, so a table and its chairs become a set. A bookcase is left as it is. Ctrl+Z takes it back.
furniture_second:
dining, coffee, side: The shape of the top. A round top has its corners cut at 45 degrees, and its legs stand in under it.
chair, stool, bench: A bare wooden seat, or one with a cushion in the upholstery colour.
armchair, sofa: Short legs under its corners, or a skirt of upholstery down to the floor.
cupboard, drawers, sideboard: A plinth set back at the front, or four feet.
chandelier: Two arms in a line, four in a cross, or four arms with two candles on each.
candlestick: One candle, or three on a bar across the stem.
bed: One pillow, or two side by side.
potted, basket, windowbox: Which plant grows in it, from the Plant form's own, or whichever the seed picks. The plant keeps its own proportions and is grown as large as the box above the soil has room for.
trellis: Which climber. Ivy is leaves alone, a clematis has flowers of one colour, a climbing rose of two, and wisteria has hanging trusses. Or a bare trellis.
furniture_seed:
bookcase: Which arrangement of books: any whole number, each a different one. Another takes the next number. The same number is always the same bookcase, and a shelf keeps its books while the bookcase is resized around it.
cupboard, drawers, sideboard, kitchen, dining, coffee, side, desk, chair, armchair, stool, bench, sofa, tablelamp, floorlamp, pendant, chandelier, sconce, candlestick, bed, potted, basket, windowbox, trellis, painting, portrait: Which piece of its style: any whole number. The seed picks among what the style allows, and Another takes the next number. The same style and seed are always the same piece, and give matching pieces of every other kind.
furniture_shine: Ticked, each lamp or flame is written to the game with a real light on it as well as glowing: a warm point light, one to a lamp and one to each candle, eight at most. Unticked, they glow and light nothing.
furniture_style: A style is a set of choices that go together. Modern: square sections, flush fronts, no mouldings. Farmhouse: turned legs, panelled doors with knobs, plank tops. Classical: tapered or turned legs, panelled doors, a cornice and a skirting, upholstery. Rustic: heavy sections, trestles and stretchers. Industrial: thin metal frames carrying slabs of wood. Random lets the seed pick one. The seed then picks among what the style allows (which leg, which back, which handle), the same way for every kind, so pieces of one style and one seed are a set. Changing the style brings its colours.
furniture_shelves: How many shelves stand between the bottom and the top. At the far left, by spacing: as many as the height has room for at the Shelf spacing, so a taller bookcase gains shelves.
furniture_size: How wide, deep or tall it is, in whole microbricks. Width and depth change about its middle and height at its top. To move one side alone, drag the dot on it. The piece is laid out again at every size: a bookcase gains shelves, a cupboard doors, a sofa seats.
furniture_spacing: The clear height wanted between one shelf and the next, in microbricks. The height inside is divided into openings as near this as whole microbricks allow, the lowest a little taller where they cannot be equal.
gif_rate: How many pictures a second a recording takes. More is smoother and a larger file. While nothing in the window changes no picture is written, whatever the rate.
gif_size: How large a recording is beside the window. Half size is a quarter of the pixels and under half the file; each pixel is the average of four of the window's.
go_to_folder: Opens this folder of saved forms in your file manager. Each save there is a .brz prefab file that the game can load as it stands.
grass_action: What a touch of the brush does to the ground under the grass. Push up raises a hill. Push down lowers the ground, below the level the patch lies on if you go on: a hollow deeper than the water stands fills with water. Flatten brings the ground to the height it has where you touch it.
grass_cliffs: How readily steep ground is a cliff. At 0 grass grows on any slope. From 1 to 3, ground steeper than a first angle is bare soil and ground steeper than a second is rock, in ledges with snow on them in the Winter colours: 52 and 68 degrees at 1, 45 and 61 at 2, 36 and 53 at 3. The grass thins as the ground steepens towards the first. A brush with a sharp edge makes ground that steep.
grass_frozen: Ticked, the pond's water is written as ice: the same bricks with their collision on, so a player stands on it, and less see-through. Choosing the Winter colours ticks it and choosing any other set unticks it.
grass_intensity: How far a push raises or lowers the ground at the middle of the brush, in microbricks. Dragging a touch's dot up or down changes it too.
grass_level: The height a flattening touch brings the ground to, in microbricks over the floor.
grass_levels: Ticked, a hollow sculpted on raised ground holds a pond of its own, each at the height its own rim gives it. A stream runs downhill from it to the nearest water that stands lower, and where the ground on the way is a cliff the stream goes over it as a waterfall, with white water where it lands. Unticked, all the water stands at one height, a little below the lawn. Which pond is high follows the ground: none is typed.
grass_passable: Ticked, the blades of grass are written with their collision off, so that a player in the game walks through them and stands on the soil underneath. Unticked, the blades are as solid as any brick.
grass_range: How far the brush reaches from where it touches. A wide brush makes a broad hill or hollow that runs smoothly into the ground round it.
grass_reeds: How thickly reeds stand in the shallows and on the bank of a pond, from none to many. A pond is any hollow pushed down deeper than the water stands.
grass_sharp: Ticked, a touch does all it does out to a narrow band at the edge of its range and falls away there: pushing up makes a table with steep sides, pushing down a pit with steep walls, and flattening a terrace with a steep bank. Those sides are steep enough for cliffs. Unticked, a touch eases off smoothly from its middle. It is a setting of the brush, for touches still to be made.
grid_at_an_angle: Bricks sit on a grid, and a grid other than the world's can stand at any angle. This grid has been turned by its rings, so everything on it is copied to the clipboard on a grid of its own. Grids pass through each other, so it is in no other grid's way.
import_colours: How many colours the mesh's own are reduced to. Each brick takes the one nearest the colour of the surface at its middle. More colours follow the model's shading more closely and cut flat areas into more bricks, since a brick is one colour. 0 leaves the mesh's colours out, and the form is coloured as any other is. The colours are listed under Colour above, where each can be changed.
import_detail: Brick size: bricks of 2 are about a quarter as many as bricks of 1, are fitted about four times as fast in an eighth of the memory, and are twice as coarse, so the model's thin parts are lost first. Automatic fits each size from the coarsest down until one goes over the Brick budget and keeps the one before, which takes several times as long as naming that size. Longest brick is how far boxes inside the model and ramps on its surface may be joined: a shorter limit is more bricks in the same shape. Every core of the processor works on finding the cells the surface passes through and the pieces that fit it; laying the pieces is done on one.
import_file: The mesh to build: a binary glTF file (.glb), a Wavefront OBJ file (.obj) or a PLY file (.ply), of up to 2 million triangles. Type or paste its path and press Enter, or drop the file on the window. The file is copied into Documents/brickloft/imports, so a saved form still opens after the original has moved. A mesh's colours are read from its points, or from a PNG picture kept inside a .glb file. A JPEG or WebP picture is not read: the mesh then has its points' colours, or none. An OBJ file's separate material and picture files are not read either.
import_fill: Ticked, everything inside the mesh's surface is brick, in boxes as large as Longest brick allows, so the inside costs few bricks. Unticked, the inside is left empty behind a wall: a few bricks fewer, and room for a player to stand inside.
import_fitter: How the bricks are chosen. Smoothed lays ramps and corner pieces in the mesh's faces, stretched to the whole-number slope nearest each face, with single pieces between them. A flat sloping face comes out exact or nearly so. A curved one comes out at under half the discrepancy cubes give and a fifth of the steps, in two to three times as many bricks and two to four times the fitting time. Blocks uses cubes alone, joined into boxes: every slope is stairs, and it is the quickest and, on a curved surface, the fewest bricks.
import_loose: Leaves out every piece of the build that touches no other piece and is smaller than this many microbricks along its longest side. A model made from one photograph often has scraps floating round it. 0 keeps everything. Pieces are judged as they are built, so a scrap that touches the body by one brick stays.
import_missing: This form's mesh file is not in Documents/brickloft/imports on this computer, so there is nothing to build it from. Open the file it came from again: the same file is given the same name, and the form finds it.
import_shell: How thick the wall of a hollow build is, in microbricks, measured inwards from the cells the surface passes through. The wall is never thinner than this and is up to 1.7 times as thick along a diagonal. Its inner face is stepped.
import_simplify: What a brick is worth, in microbricks of disagreement with the mesh. At 0 a stretched piece is laid only where it is at least as close to the mesh as the single pieces it replaces. Above 0 it may be further from the mesh by this much for every brick it saves. At 0.25 a curved model is about a third fewer bricks at nearly twice the discrepancy, with a fifth more steps; above 0.5 it gains nothing more. It changes nothing for Blocks.
import_size: How long the mesh's longest side is, in microbricks. The dot in the view sets it by dragging. At twice the size the surface has about four times the bricks and takes four times as long to fit, in eight times the memory, and the bricks follow the surface more closely, since they are the same size on a larger model. A mesh drawn in whole units is built exactly where its size is its length in those units.
import_up: Which of the file's axes points up. glTF says Y, and most OBJ files follow it. A PLY file does not say, and is taken to have Z up until this is changed. Changing it reads the file again. For any other turn, use Quarter turn below.
leaves_passable: Ticked, the plant's greenery (leaves, needles, fronds, petals, berries, baubles) is written with its collision off, so a player walks through the crown, and its wood (trunk, limbs, stems) stays solid. Unticked, all of it is solid.
line_up: Gives the arch a grid of its own, turned so that the arch runs straight along it, with its feet left where they are. Bricks on a grid at an angle are fitted as if it were level, so the arch comes out as smooth as any other. Ctrl+Z takes it back.
longest_brick: The longest edge a single brick may have, in microbricks. 80 is what the game was seen to accept when this was first tried; the game's own limit is said to be 800 studs, which is 4000 microbricks. Raise it and paste to find out: a form then needs fewer, longer bricks.
maze_divisions: How many cells the first ring round the room is cut into by spokes. Fewer are used if that many would not leave room to pass between them.
maze_entrance: Where on the rim the way in is, in degrees round from the X axis. The cell of the outermost ring at that angle is opened to the outside.
maze_floor: A floor under the whole maze, this many microbricks thick, out to the outside of its rim. The walls stand on it. It is the first of the maze's colours.
maze_gap: From the middle of one ring wall to the middle of the next: a corridor and one wall. Changing it keeps the number of rings and resizes the maze. The dot on the rim does the same by dragging. A corridor is never less than 3 microbricks between its walls.
maze_grow: How the number of cells in a ring grows outwards. Left to keep cells square, a ring has twice the cells of the ring inside it wherever its cells would otherwise be more than twice as wide as the corridor. Otherwise it doubles every so many rings, as long as there is room to pass between the spokes. It only ever doubles, so every spoke of a ring lines up with a spoke of the ring outside it.
maze_height: How tall the walls stand above the floor. The dot over the middle of the maze does the same by dragging. A hedge is never under 12.
maze_kind: Which maze. Theta is rings of corridors about a round room, with walls that are arcs and spokes. Grid is square cells about a square room. Either has one way in, on its rim, and one way to the room in the middle; every part of it can be reached, and there are no loops.
maze_rings: How many rings the maze has, the room in the middle counted as the first. Changing it keeps the corridors as wide as they are, so the maze grows or shrinks. A grid has this many cells from its middle to its edge.
maze_seed: Which maze: any whole number, each a different one. Another takes the next number. The same number and settings are always the same maze.
maze_solution: Lays a strip one microbrick high along the ground from the way in to the room in the middle, in a colour of its own: the last of the maze's colours, or the third if its walls are plain. Untick it before copying a maze that is meant to be solved.
maze_texture: What the walls are made of. None is plain walls in one colour. Hedge grows the Plant form's hedge along every wall, with its own density, looseness and berries; it is at least 6 thick and 12 tall, and is tens of thousands of bricks. Planks, bricks, cobblestone and medallions are wrapped along each wall: courses of bricks run level along a wall and bend round the rings with it. A texture colours the walls and never moves them, so the long sloped bricks of a curved face are each one colour to a course. Choosing a texture brings its colours unless you have set your own: the first is the floor and the mortar, the last the strip that marks the way through.
mirror: Make the form its own mirror image along an axis: its low side along that axis is kept, and the high side becomes its mirror image, about the middle of the form's dots. An arch with one foot higher than the other gets two feet alike; a point added to one side of a circle appears on the other too.
natural_height: Ticked, the arch takes the height its shape gives it: a round arch is a semicircle. Dragging the top dot sets your own height.
neighbouring_dots_follow: How much of a dragged dot's movement the dots near it share: 0 moves it alone, 1 takes its nearest neighbours almost all the way with it. The share falls away with distance, out to three times the reach of added points.
new_grid: A new cube on a grid of its own, which its rings turn to any angle and its arrows move, apart from every other grid.
pattern: A texture to lay the form as, in place of plain brick. Stepping stones are separate stones of any shape, or with the gap at 0 stones fitted together, each sharing its edges with the stones round it. Medallions repeats a few ringed figures over the whole floor. Rug is a Persian carpet: nested borders, a lobed medallion with pendants, corner pieces, and scrolling stems with flowers and leaves. Planks is a floor of boards. Bricks is courses of bricks, every one a rectangle. Cobblestone is stones of any shape fitted together. Both can be as uneven as you ask, with or without mortar. Stepping stones need a flat form. The others colour the form without reshaping it: they are laid through a flat form, on the flat part of a form that is not flat all over, and on the sides of a box. Choosing a pattern brings its colours with it unless you have set your own: the first colour is the ground or the mortar, and the others are shared among the pattern's parts, up to eight. An arch also offers hedge, which builds it as clipped hedge with the hedge's own density, looseness, berries and seed.
pattern_bevel: Slopes the top microbrick of every brick down to its edge, all round it, with the mortar at the foot of the slope. It needs the form to be 2 or more deep, and is cut into one face: the top of a floor.
pattern_border: How many microbricks of plain ground are left round the edge of the pattern.
pattern_grooved: Slopes the last microbrick of every row of boards down to the next row, so that each row stands one microbrick proud of the one beside it along a straight line. It needs boards of size 3 or more and a form 2 or more deep, and is cut into one face: the top of a floor.
pattern_mortar: Whether there is a microbrick of mortar between one piece and the next. Without it they touch, and are told apart by their shades alone, so give the pattern several colours.
pattern_seed: Which one of the pattern: any whole number, each a different one. Another takes the next number and the next of the pattern's sets of colours.
pattern_size: How large the boards, bricks or cobbles are. 2 is the usual size, 1 half of it and 4 twice.
pattern_stagger: How far each course is moved along from the one before, as a share of a brick's length. 50% is the usual half-brick bond, 0% stacks the bricks in columns, and 25% or 33% make the joints step across the wall.
pattern_stagger_uneven: Moves each course along by an amount of its own, so that the upright joints fall anywhere. Untick it to set one stagger for every course.
pattern_sunk: Lays the mortar one microbrick below the stones, which stand proud of it with upright sides. It needs the form to be 2 or more deep, and is cut into one face: the top of a floor.
pattern_uneven_across: How unlike one another the pieces are across the courses. For bricks it moves the lines between courses, so that the courses differ in depth. For cobbles it moves each stone's point up and down.
pattern_uneven_along: How unlike one another the pieces are along the courses. For bricks it moves the joints, so that the bricks differ in length and stay rectangles. For cobbles it moves each stone's point from side to side.
pattern_upright: Runs the courses up the floor instead of across it, so that the bricks stand on end and the stagger is from side to side.
pine_baubles: How many baubles hang on the tree, from none to one under the end and the middle of nearly every bough. They are of three sizes and three of the tree's colours, none touching another, and metal in the game.
pine_hang: How far from the stem the tinsel is wound, as a share of the way out to the ends of the boughs. Low, it is tight round the tree among the boughs; at 100% it lies on their ends; above that it hangs clear of them.
pine_lights: None; a string of lights wound round the tree; or candles standing on the ends of its boughs. A tree has 40 at most. Each is a glowing brick.
pine_shine: Ticked, every light or candle flame is written with a small warm light on it, so the tree lights what is round it in the game. Each light costs the game a little to draw: untick this to keep the glowing bricks without the lights.
pine_star: A five-pointed star on the top of the tree. In the game it is metal.
pine_tinsel: A garland of tinsel wound down round the tree from its top, sagging between the boughs it lies on. It is metal in the game.
pyramid_height: The pyramid's height. Left alone it is as tall as half its base is wide.
quarter_turn: Turn the form a quarter turn about an axis, within the brick grid. The form is the same bricks whichever way it faces. For any other angle, drag one of the red, green or blue rings round: that turns the form's whole grid.
radius: The form's size from its middle to its edge, in microbricks. Ctrl + scroll over the view changes it too.
ramps_and_corners: Unticked, the form is built of cubes alone, as a staircase.
record_gif: Records the window as an animated GIF, saved in Pictures/brickloft under the date and time when you stop. F11 does the same, and Shift+F11 leaves this panel out. A red dot in the corner of the view shows while it records; the dot is not in the recording. A recording stops by itself at 60 seconds or 64 MB.
reach_of_added_points: How far from each added point the form goes with it: along a curve to either side, or all round on a sphere or pyramid.
remove_form: Take the form being edited out of the workspace.
reset_form: Put the dots, sizes, stretch, flips and other choices back to how this form starts out. How it is fitted and coloured is left alone.
round_tube: Builds the curve as a round tube, which for a circle is a torus. Unticked it is a flat band with a thickness and a depth.
save_report: Writes out this form's settings, its bricks, and a cell-by-cell comparison of the bricks with the form: where material is missing or extra. Useful for working out why a fit looks wrong. Reports go in the folder brickloft in the system's temporary folder. If the editor ever closes by itself, brickloft-crash.txt in that folder says why.
save_screenshot: Saves a picture of the window in Pictures/brickloft and puts it on the clipboard. F12 does the same, and Shift+F12 leaves this panel out of the picture.
saved_add: Add its forms to the workspace, beside the form being edited and on its grid.
saved_delete: Delete this saved form. You are asked first.
saved_drag: Drag onto the view to add it to the workspace.
saved_folder: The folder of saved forms shown below. Add folder makes a new one.
saved_forms: A save holds the whole workspace: every form, with its colours and the grid it is on.
saved_open: Open in place of everything in the workspace. Ctrl+Z brings the workspace back.
saved_save: Saves the whole workspace under this name in the chosen folder: every form, with its colours and the grid it is on. A save of the same name is replaced.
segment_from: Where the segment starts, measured up from the sphere's centre.
segment_to: Where the segment ends, measured up from the sphere's centre.
sharp_corners: Ticked, the hedge, reeds or grass runs straight from dot to dot and turns a corner at each. Unticked, it follows a smooth curve through them.
show_parts: What is drawn over the bricks, each switched on its own. Rulers give the form's size along each axis in microbricks. Rings turn the form's grid to any angle. Arrows move the form being edited, and any picked with it, along one axis. Dots are the form's own points and sizes, which you drag to reshape it. Anything hidden cannot be taken hold of either, so it is never in the way.
simplify: How much closer a ramp must bring the outline to be worth a brick, in microbricks of area. 0 is the closest fit whatever the count; higher gives fewer, longer pieces. Flat forms only: on a 3D form, use Brick size.
sliders_go_up_to: How far every size slider reaches, in microbricks: radius, height, thickness, depth and the reach of added points. Lower it for a finer slider. Large forms take longer to fit.
snap_after_every_drag: Runs Snap to best fit nearby by itself each time a drag ends.
snap_best_fit: A form fits cleanly only where its surfaces land on the brick grid. This tries each dot and size up to a microbrick either way and keeps whatever fits closest.
snap_half_microbricks: Dots snap to half microbricks, which are single game units. Unticked they snap to whole microbricks.
solid_cube: Solid all through, or hollow with walls as thick as Wall thickness on every side. A hollow box too short to have a hollow inside is open through its shortest length: a frame.
solid_pyramid: Solid all through, or a hollow tent open underneath.
solid_revolve: Solid all through, or a shell along the profile as thick as Wall thickness: a vase or a bowl.
solid_sphere: Solid all through, or a hollow shell as thick as Wall thickness.
sphere_keep: The whole sphere, a dome (its top half), or a segment between two heights.
stone_gap: How wide the gap between neighbouring stones is, in microbricks. At 0 the stones are fitted together with no gap, as in a stone wall or a paved floor: two stones share the edge between them, and their corners are sharp where with a gap they are rounded.
stone_size: About how far apart the middles of neighbouring stones are, in microbricks. A stone is a little under this across.
stone_uneven: 0 gives stones as alike in size as scattered stones can be. 1 gives some crowded small and others left large.
stretch: Stretches the form along this axis: 2 makes it twice as long that way, 0.5 half as long.
stretch_circle: Stretches the circle along this axis into an ellipse: 2 makes it twice as long that way, 0.5 half as long. How thick a ring or a round tube is, is its Thickness.
stripe_width: How wide each stripe is, in microbricks.
thickness: How thick the band, the tube or the wall is, in microbricks.
tree_bend:
pine: How far its boughs droop.
palm, datepalm: How far its trunk leans.
oak, beech, birch, willow, scotspine, cherry: How crooked its limbs are.
boxwood, hedge, hydrangea, cypress: How uneven its outline is, from freshly clipped to grown out.
peony: How open its bloom is, from a round bud to full blown.
sunflower: How far its head nods.
tulip: How open its cup is.
petunia: How far it trails from the mound.
reeds: How far the stems lean and their leaves flop.
yucca: How far its blades bend over.
bed: How unevenly its flowers stand.
daisy, daffodil: This setting does nothing for this flower.
grass: How far the blades lean.
flower: How open the bloom is, from a closed bud at 0 through half open to full blown at 100. Its petals lean out, uncurl and roll back their lips as it opens.
tree_colours: A set of colours for the plant's parts: bark or stem, three greens, limbs, and its petals, blooms or extras. Pines have a set under snow, oaks have autumn sets, and peonies and tulips come in several colours. Change any colour below to make a set of your own.
tree_count:
pine: How many tiers of boughs the tree has.
palm, datepalm: How many fronds are in its crown.
oak: How many limbs its trunk divides into.
beech, birch, willow, scotspine, cherry: How many main limbs leave its stem.
boxwood: How many stems it stands on.
hedge: How many plants stand along it.
peony: How many stems stand in the clump, each with one bloom.
sunflower, tulip, daisy, daffodil: How many flowers stand in the clump, each a different height.
hydrangea: How many flower heads it carries.
petunia: How many flowers it has.
reeds: How many stems stand in it.
yucca: How many blades are in its rosette.
bed: How many flowers stand in the bed.
cypress: A cypress has nothing to count.
grass: How far below the lawn water stands in a hollow, in microbricks; 0 for no water.
flower: A single flower has nothing to count.
tree_extras:
palm: A cluster of coconuts under the crown.
datepalm: Bunches of dates under the crown.
boxwood, hedge: Berries among the leaves, in the seventh colour.
oak, beech, birch, willow, scotspine: Ticked, the tree is bare, with twigs where its leaves were.
cherry: Ticked, the tree is bare, with no blossom.
reeds: The feathery plumes of common reed in place of a bulrush's brown heads.
yucca: Its tall stalk of cream bells.
flower: The green under the bloom, which are a rose's five sepals (they lie against the bud and turn back as it opens), a water lily's four, or a gerbera's ring of small bracts. Unticked, the bloom is petals alone.
tree_fullness:
pine: How many boughs it has and how wide their sprays are.
palm, datepalm: How long its leaflets are.
oak, beech, birch: How large its masses of leaves are, with less sky between them.
willow: How large its masses of leaves are and how thick its hanging curtains.
cherry: How thick its blossom is.
scotspine: How large its plates of needles are.
boxwood, hedge, cypress: How thick its canopy is.
peony: How many petals and leaves it has.
sunflower: How large its petals and leaves are.
tulip: How large its leaves are.
hydrangea, petunia, reeds, daisy, daffodil, bed: How leafy it is.
yucca: How wide its blades are.
grass: How thickly the blades grow.
flower: How many petals it has, which is from 10 to 30 for a rose, from 14 to 36 for a water lily, and 13, 21 or 34 rays in each of a gerbera's two rows.
tree_girth: How thick the trunk is, from half of what is usual for the tree's kind and height to twice it. The limbs that leave the trunk are thicker or thinner with it, and so are a palm's rings and swollen foot. A trunk is never made thinner than bricks can show: about three microbricks through.
tree_height: How tall the plant is, in microbricks. The dot at its top sets it too. Its twigs and petals are a microbrick or two thick at any size, so a tall plant has more detail than a short one. A single flower's height is how deep its bloom is, from its foot to the top of its petals in bud. Made taller or shorter than is usual for its width, the bloom is deeper or shallower.
tree_kind: Which plant. Trees: a pine (a spruce, the Christmas tree), a Scots pine, a coconut palm, a date palm, an oak, a beech, a birch, a weeping willow, a cherry in blossom. Bushes: a boxwood, a hedge of it, a hydrangea, a cypress, a yucca. Flowers: a peony, sunflowers, tulips, petunias, daisies, daffodils, a bed of mixed flowers, and a single flower, which is one large bloom with no plant under it. And reeds and grass. Each is grown its own way. Choosing one starts it at its usual size and in its own colours.
tree_seed: Which plant of its kind: any whole number, each a different one. Another takes the next number. The same number is always the same plant.
tree_spread:
pine, scotspine: How far its longest boughs reach to each side. The dot at its side sets it too.
palm, datepalm: How long its fronds are. The dot at its side sets it too.
oak, beech, birch, willow, cherry: How far its crown reaches to each side. The dot at its side sets it too.
boxwood, hydrangea, cypress, yucca, petunia: How far the plant reaches to each side. The dot at its side sets it too.
hedge, reeds: Half its thickness, across its line. The dot at its side sets it too.
grass: How far the lawn reaches to each side of its line, where the line is not a closed outline.
sunflower, daisy: Half the width of a flower's head; the clump is wider. The dot at its side sets it too.
tulip, daffodil, peony: Half the width of a flower's cup or bloom; the clump is wider. The dot at its side sets it too.
bed: How far the bed reaches to each side. The dot at its side sets it too.
flower: Half the width of the bloom when it is full blown; less open, it is narrower. The dot at its side sets it too.
tube_protruded: Flat bands side by side, each standing proud of the next.
tube_rounded: A pipe: the edges chamfered round with sloped pieces.
tube_section: How a round tube's section is made. Rounded is a pipe with chamfered edges. Protruded is flat bands of different widths side by side: smooth along the curve and stepped across it.
whole_circle: Builds the whole circle through the three points, where unticked it is the arc from the first point to the last.
workspace: Forms stand on grids. Forms on one grid are kept clear of each other and are turned together by the rings. The arrows move the form being edited and any picked with it (Shift + click), and the whole grid when all of it is picked. Hold Ctrl while dragging a form to move it into another instead: the two are then one build, fitted afresh where they meet. Grids pass through each other.
workspace_buttons: Add to this grid sets a new cube beside the forms on this grid: they are kept clear of each other and turn together. New grid gives the new cube a grid of its own, which its rings turn to any angle. Duplicate adds a copy of the form being edited to its grid, in the same colours. Remove takes the form being edited out of the workspace.
workspace_form: Edit this form, and its grid. Clicking it in the view does the same.
furniture_cover: How much of the trellis the climber covers: at the left a young plant with a few short stems, at the right an old one that has nearly reached the top. The lattice always shows through it.
program: Which rule program the form runs. A rule program starts from an empty grid of cells and changes it a little each turn by rewrite rules, until a building stands in it. Each cell is then built as a block of microbricks. The language and the programs listed are MarkovJunior's, by Maxim Gumin (github.com/mxgmn/MarkovJunior, MIT licence). CarmaTower is a proceduralization of a voxel scene by Antoine Lendrevie. Choosing a program sets its usual grid and its own colours.
program_import: Brings in a rule program someone has written: the path of its .xml file, typed or pasted here, then Import. Dropping the file on the window does the same. The program and the files it reads (its tileset, its tiles and its rules kept as .vox files) are copied into Documents/brickloft/programs, so a save that names it opens again. Those files are looked for beside the .xml file and in a folder called resources beside it, then among the ones that come with the editor. A program that uses a part of the language this editor does not run is refused, and the message names the part and its line.
program_size: How many cells the program's starting grid has along X, Y and Z. A larger grid is a larger building and a longer run. Some programs build several cells for each cell of this grid, so the finished grid can be five times this size each way. Usual puts back the size the program was written for. A program made for flat pictures wants a Z of 1.
program_cell: How many microbricks each cell of the finished grid is built across. It changes the size of the building and nothing about its shape, and the program is not run again for it.
program_seed: Which of the program's buildings this is. The same program, grid and seed give the same building on every computer. Another takes the next seed. Some seeds cannot be finished (the program finds no way to fit its tiles together): the editor then goes on to the next seed by itself and says below which seeds it passed over.
program_finish: Plain cells builds each cell as a cube and nothing else. With wedges also reads the grid for flights of steps and fills the notch above each step with a ramp, so a staircase becomes one slope a player walks up without jumping, and stepped roofs get corner pieces. No cell is removed either way.
program_limit: The most turns a run may take. A program that loops, or a grid too large to finish in reasonable time, is stopped here: what it had made stays on screen and a message says it stopped early. Raise the limit to let a long run go on.
program_colours: Puts the form's colours back to the program's own: one colour for each letter the program uses, from MarkovJunior's palette. Each colour in the Colour list above can be changed like any other form's.
program_play: Play runs the program from where it stands, a few turns each frame, and Pause stops it there. A paused run is a form like any other: the bricks on screen are what is copied, saved and joined, and a save of it opens at the same turn. Play on a finished run starts it again from the first turn.
program_restart: Starts the run again from an empty grid with the same seed, and plays it.
program_to_end: Runs on to the end without drawing the turns between.
program_speed: How many turns are taken each second while the run plays. A program takes from about a hundred turns to a few thousand. A turn that needs longer than its share of a second is waited for, and the window keeps answering meanwhile.
program_watch: Ticked, a change of program, grid, seed or step limit is played from its first turn. Unticked, the change is shown finished, with no animation.
program_working: One turn of a program can take a second or more: the first turn of a wave function collapse node tries seeds until one fills the grid. The turn is taken behind the window, which keeps answering, and the building appears when it is done.
